course.title: Biostatistics
course.description: Biostatistics applies statistical reasoning to biology, medicine, and public health, turning the noisy data from studies and experiments into conclusions you can actually trust. You will work through data types and study designs, descriptive statistics, probability and the normal distribution, sampling and confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, correlation and regression, risk measures, and the bias and confounding that can mislead. Structure adapted from Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (CC BY-SA 4.0).

options: applying statistics to biology, medicine, and health
writing clinical case notes by hand
questions.explanation: Biostatistics designs biological and health studies and analyzes their data - see 'Why biology and medicine need statistics'.

questions.explanation: Randomized assignment is the defining feature of a randomized controlled trial.

questions.prompt: The middle value of an ordered data set is the...
questions.explanation: The median is the central value once the data are sorted.

questions.prompt: In a normal distribution, about what percent of values lie within 1 SD of the mean?
questions.explanation: The empirical rule: about 68% within 1 SD, 95% within 2 SD, 99.7% within 3 SD.

options: contains 95% of the raw data points
gives a plausible range for the true parameter at the 95% level
questions.explanation: A confidence interval is a range of plausible values for the unknown parameter, not a range of individuals.

options: the probability the null hypothesis is true
the probability of data at least as extreme as observed, assuming the null is true
the chance of a type II error
questions.explanation: A p-value is computed assuming the null hypothesis holds; it is not the probability the null is true.

questions.explanation: A type I error is a false positive - rejecting a true null.

questions.explanation: A confounder can create or hide an apparent link - see 'Reading results responsibly'.

lessons.title: Why biology and medicine need statistics
lessons.grammar_note: A parameter describes a whole population and is usually unknown; a statistic is computed from a sample and only estimates it. Keep the two words apart.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain what biostatistics is, why living systems demand statistical thinking, and how a research question becomes a measurable study. You will separate a population from a sample, and a parameter from a statistic. Warm-up: if one patient improves after taking a new drug, why is that not yet evidence that the drug works?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Biostatistics is the branch of statistics that designs biological experiments and studies, then collects, analyzes, and interprets the data they produce. It exists because living systems vary: two patients given the same dose respond differently, and two samples from the same population rarely give the same number. That variation means a single result can be luck rather than signal. Statistics separates the two by thinking in terms of a population - every unit we care about - and a sample drawn from it. A number describing the whole population, like the true mean blood pressure, is a parameter; the matching number from a sample is a statistic, which only estimates the parameter. Because the estimate carries uncertainty, biostatistics attaches a measure of that uncertainty to every conclusion. The same tools serve clinical trials, epidemiology, genetics, agriculture, and ecology. The workflow is always the same: state a clear question, choose a design that can answer it, collect data, summarize it, and quantify how much the numbers let you conclude.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Turn vague questions into measurable ones. 'Does this drug work?' becomes 'In adults with high blood pressure, does drug X lower systolic pressure more than a placebo over 12 weeks?' Now you can measure the difference in mean pressure and test it. 'Is coffee bad for you?' becomes 'Among adults, is daily coffee intake associated with a higher rate of heart disease over 10 years, holding age and smoking fixed?' Second, population versus sample: the true average height of all adults in a country is a parameter you cannot observe, so you measure 1,000 people and compute the sample mean, a statistic. If a second sample of 1,000 gives a slightly different mean, that gap is sampling variation, not a real change in the country. Third, signal versus noise: if 6 of 10 treated patients improve versus 5 of 10 controls, the one-patient gap is well within what chance alone produces, so it is not yet evidence. Larger samples shrink the noise and let a real effect show.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Rewrite 'is exercise good?' as a measurable question. 2) Is the average recovery time of all surgery patients a parameter or a statistic? 3) You sample 50 people twice and get means 70 and 72 kg; name the cause of the gap. 4) True or false: one improved patient proves a treatment works. 5) Why attach uncertainty to every estimate? Answers: 1) e.g. 'Among sedentary adults, does 30 minutes of walking 5 days a week lower resting heart rate over 8 weeks versus no change?' 2) a parameter, since it describes the whole population. 3) sampling variation - different samples give different means. 4) false; it could easily be chance, and there is no comparison group. 5) because a sample only estimates the population, so the number could be off, and the size of that possible error matters for any decision.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating a sample statistic as if it were the exact population parameter - it is an estimate with error. Mistake: concluding that a treatment works from before-and-after change in one group, with no comparison and no account of chance. Mistake: asking a question too vague to measure, so no design can answer it. Exit: (a) What is the difference between a parameter and a statistic? (b) Why can a single improved patient not establish that a drug works? Answers: a parameter describes the whole population and is usually unknown, while a statistic is computed from a sample and estimates it; a single case has no comparison group and is easily explained by chance or natural recovery, so it carries almost no evidence on its own.

lessons.title: Types of data and study designs
lessons.grammar_note: Observational studies watch what already happens; experiments assign the exposure. Only an experiment, through randomization, can balance unknown confounders by itself.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Classify data as categorical or numerical, and tell apart the main study designs - cross-sectional, cohort, case-control, and the randomized controlled trial. You will match each design to the question it can answer. Warm-up: if smokers have more lung cancer than non-smokers, why can we not yet say that smoking caused it?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Data come in two broad types. Categorical data put each unit in a group: nominal (blood type, with no order) or ordinal (pain rated mild, moderate, severe, which has order but no fixed spacing). Numerical data are counts or measurements: discrete (number of seizures) or continuous (weight, which can take any value in a range). The type decides which summary and which test fit. Study designs split into observational and experimental. In observational designs the researcher only watches. A cross-sectional study takes a snapshot at one time. A cohort study follows groups defined by exposure forward in time to see who develops the outcome. A case-control study starts from the outcome - cases with the disease and controls without - and looks backward at exposure, which is efficient for rare diseases. In an experiment the researcher assigns the exposure. The randomized controlled trial (RCT) randomly allots participants to treatment or control; randomization balances both known and unknown confounders on average, which is why the RCT is the strongest design for cause.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Classify: blood type is nominal categorical; tumor stage I to IV is ordinal; number of hospital visits is discrete numerical; serum cholesterol is continuous numerical. Match the design to the question. To test a new vaccine, randomly assign volunteers to vaccine or placebo and compare infection rates - an RCT. To study whether a rare birth defect is linked to a medication, collect babies with the defect (cases) and without (controls) and compare past medication use - a case-control study, efficient because the defect is rare. To estimate how many adults currently have diabetes, survey a sample once - cross-sectional. To see whether a diet raises heart-disease risk, enroll healthy people, record diet, and follow them for 10 years - a cohort study. Why the smoking example stalls: in observational data, smokers may also differ in diet, exercise, and income, any of which could drive the cancer. Those are confounders, and only a design that balances them - ideally randomization - lets you claim cause rather than association.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Is 'eye color' nominal or ordinal? 2) Is 'number of cavities' discrete or continuous? 3) Which design follows exposed and unexposed groups forward in time? 4) Which design is best for a rare disease, starting from who has it? 5) Why does randomization help with unknown confounders? 6) True or false: a cross-sectional study can show that exposure came before disease. Answers: 1) nominal - no natural order. 2) discrete - you count whole cavities. 3) a cohort study. 4) a case-control study. 5) random assignment makes the groups similar on average for every variable, measured or not, so differences in the outcome are more credibly due to the treatment. 6) false - a single snapshot cannot establish time order, so it is weak for cause.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: reading an observed association as proof of cause - 'associated with' is not 'causes.' Mistake: treating ordinal categories as if their gaps were equal, then averaging them without care. Mistake: confusing a cohort study (start from exposure, look forward) with a case-control study (start from outcome, look back). Exit: (a) Name the two broad data types and give one example of each. (b) Which study design most convincingly supports a causal claim, and why? Answers: categorical (for example, blood type) and numerical (for example, weight); the randomized controlled trial, because randomly assigning the exposure balances known and unknown confounders across the groups, so a difference in outcome can be attributed to the treatment.

lessons.title: Descriptive statistics: center, spread, and shape
lessons.grammar_note: The mean is pulled toward extreme values; the median is not. For a skewed measurement like income or hospital cost, report the median.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Summarize a data set with measures of center (mean, median, mode) and spread (range, variance, SD), and read the shape of a distribution from a histogram. Warm-up: if one billionaire walks into a small cafe, does the mean or the median income of the room change more?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Descriptive statistics compress many numbers into a few that capture center, spread, and shape. The mean is the arithmetic average: add the values and divide by the count. The median is the middle value once the data are ordered; with an even count, average the two middle values. The mode is the most frequent value. The mean uses every number but is dragged by outliers, while the median resists them, so for skewed data the median describes the typical case better. Spread matters as much as center. The range is max minus min. The variance is the average squared distance from the mean, and the standard deviation (SD) is its square root, back in the original units, so it reads as a typical distance from the mean. Shape is seen in a histogram: symmetric and bell-like, or skewed with a long tail on one side. In a right-skewed distribution the mean sits above the median. Always report a center together with a spread; a mean alone hides how varied the data are.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Take the values 2, 4, 4, 6, 9. Mean = (2 + 4 + 4 + 6 + 9) / 5 = 25 / 5 = 5. Ordered, the middle value is 4, so the median = 4. The mode is 4, since it appears twice. Range = 9 - 2 = 7. For the SD, find each deviation from the mean 5: -3, -1, -1, 1, 4; square them: 9, 1, 1, 1, 16; their average is 28 / 5 = 5.6 (the variance), and SD = square root of 5.6, about 2.37. Now add an outlier, 100: the mean jumps to 125 / 6, about 20.8, but the median only moves to 5. That gap is why skewed data - incomes, hospital charges, survival times - are usually reported with the median. Reading shape: if mean >= median by a lot, suspect a right (positive) skew with a long high tail; if the mean is close to the median, the data look roughly symmetric.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Find the mean of 3, 7, 7, 9. 2) Find the median of 1, 3, 8, 10. 3) What is the mode of 5, 5, 6, 9, 9, 9? 4) Give the range of 12, 4, 20, 8. 5) If the mean is far above the median, what shape is likely? 6) Why report the SD alongside the mean? Answers: 1) 26 / 4 = 6.5. 2) average of 3 and 8 = 5.5. 3) 9. 4) 20 - 4 = 16. 5) right-skewed, with a long upper tail. 6) the mean alone hides spread; the SD says how far values typically fall from it, so two groups with the same mean can still be very different.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: reporting the mean for strongly skewed data, where it misstates the typical value - use the median. Mistake: confusing variance (squared units) with SD (original units); only the SD is directly comparable to the data. Mistake: giving a center with no spread, so readers cannot judge variability. Exit: (a) For right-skewed hospital costs, should you report the mean or the median, and why? (b) What does the standard deviation measure? Answers: the median, because a few very large bills pull the mean upward and overstate the typical cost; the standard deviation measures the typical distance of a value from the mean, in the same units as the data, summarizing how spread out the values are.

lessons.title: Probability and the normal distribution
lessons.grammar_note: A probability is always between 0 and 1. The 68-95-99.7 rule applies only to a normal (bell-shaped) distribution, not to every data set.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Use basic probability rules and the normal distribution to say how likely a measurement is, and convert a value to a z-score. Warm-up: in a bell curve, roughly what fraction of values sit within 2 SD of the mean?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Probability measures how likely an event is, on a scale from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). For equally likely outcomes, probability = favorable outcomes / total outcomes. Two rules do most of the work. The addition rule: for events that cannot both happen (mutually exclusive), P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B). The multiplication rule: for independent events, P(A and B) = P(A) times P(B). Many biological measurements - height, blood pressure, measurement error - follow an approximately normal distribution, the symmetric bell curve described by its mean and SD. The empirical rule says about 68% of values fall within 1 SD of the mean, about 95% within 2 SD, and about 99.7% within 3 SD. To compare a value to the curve, convert it to a z-score: z = (value - mean) / SD, which counts how many SDs the value lies from the mean. A positive z is above the mean, a negative z below. The normal distribution matters because, as the next lesson shows, sample means tend toward it even when the raw data do not.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Probability basics: a fair die shows an even number with probability 3 / 6 = 0.5. Rolling two independent dice, P(both six) = (1 / 6) times (1 / 6) = 1 / 36, about 0.028, by the multiplication rule. Drawing one card, P(heart or spade) = 13 / 52 + 13 / 52 = 0.5, by the addition rule, since a card cannot be both. Normal distribution: suppose adult systolic blood pressure is roughly normal with mean 120 and SD 10. A reading of 140 has z = (140 - 120) / 10 = 2.0, so it sits 2 SD above the mean; by the empirical rule only about 2.5% of people are above that, half of the 5% outside 2 SD. A reading of 110 has z = (110 - 120) / 10 = -1.0, one SD below the mean. About 68% of readings lie between 110 and 130 (mean plus or minus 1 SD), and about 95% between 100 and 140.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What is the probability of rolling an odd number on a fair die? 2) P(two independent coin flips both land heads)? 3) Mean 50, SD 5: find the z-score of 60. 4) Roughly what percent of normal values lie within 1 SD of the mean? 5) What does a z-score of 0 mean? 6) Is a probability of 1.4 possible? Answers: 1) 3 / 6 = 0.5. 2) 0.5 times 0.5 = 0.25. 3) z = (60 - 50) / 5 = 2.0. 4) about 68%. 5) the value equals the mean, zero SDs away. 6) no - probabilities must lie between 0 and 1, so 1.4 signals an error.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: adding probabilities of events that can happen together, or multiplying ones that are not independent - check the condition first. Mistake: applying the 68-95-99.7 rule to data that are not normal; the rule is a property of the bell curve only. Mistake: forgetting the sign of a z-score, which tells you above or below the mean. Exit: (a) What does a z-score of 2 mean? (b) What fraction of a normal distribution lies within 2 SD of the mean? Answers: the value is 2 standard deviations above the mean; about 95% of the distribution falls within 2 SD of the mean, leaving roughly 2.5% in each tail.

questions.explanation: A parameter describes the population; a statistic estimates it from a sample.

questions.prompt: Which design randomly assigns participants to treatment or control?
questions.explanation: Randomization is what defines the randomized controlled trial and balances confounders.

questions.explanation: A few very large values pull the mean up, so the median describes the typical case.

questions.explanation: SD is the square root of the variance, returning to the original units.

questions.prompt: In a normal distribution, about 95% of values lie within how many SD of the mean?
questions.explanation: The empirical rule: about 95% within 2 SD of the mean.

questions.prompt: A z-score of -1.5 means the value is...
questions.explanation: A negative z-score sits below the mean; here by 1.5 standard deviations.

lessons.title: Sampling and confidence intervals
lessons.grammar_note: The standard deviation describes spread among individuals; the standard error describes spread among sample means. The standard error shrinks as the sample grows.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain how a sample represents a population, describe the sampling distribution of the mean, and build and read a confidence interval. Warm-up: why does a mean from 1,000 people vary less between samples than a mean from 10 people?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A sample is useful only if it represents the population, so good sampling avoids bias - a convenience sample of volunteers can skew results. Imagine taking many samples of the same size and computing each one's mean. Those means form the sampling distribution of the mean. The central limit theorem says that, as the sample size n grows, this distribution becomes approximately normal and centers on the true population mean, even when the raw data are not normal. Its spread is the standard error, SE = SD / square root of n, which shrinks as n grows - bigger samples give steadier estimates. A confidence interval turns one sample into a range of plausible values for the parameter. For a mean, an approximate 95% interval is sample mean plus or minus about 2 times SE. The '95% confidence' refers to the method: if you repeated the whole process many times, about 95% of the intervals built this way would contain the true mean. A wider interval means more uncertainty; larger samples give narrower intervals.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Suppose a sample of n = 100 patients has mean cholesterol 200 with SD 40. The standard error is SE = 40 / square root of 100 = 40 / 10 = 4. An approximate 95% confidence interval is 200 plus or minus 2 times 4, that is 200 plus or minus 8, or 192 to 208. We are 95% confident, in the method sense, that the true mean lies in that range. Now raise the sample to n = 400 with the same SD: SE = 40 / 20 = 2, and the interval narrows to 200 plus or minus 4, or 196 to 204 - four times the data halves the width. Interpreting correctly: the interval 192 to 208 does not mean 95% of patients have cholesterol in that range; it is a statement about the unknown mean. And if a second sample gave a mean of 205, that is ordinary sampling variation, well inside the interval.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) SD = 20, n = 100. Find the standard error. 2) With mean 50 and that SE, give an approximate 95% confidence interval. 3) Does quadrupling n halve or quarter the SE? 4) True or false: a 95% CI means 95% of individuals fall inside it. 5) What makes a confidence interval narrower? Answers: 1) SE = 20 / square root of 100 = 2. 2) 50 plus or minus 2 times 2 = 50 plus or minus 4, so 46 to 54. 3) halve it - the SE depends on the square root of n. 4) false; it is a statement about the parameter, not individuals. 5) a larger sample (or less variability) shrinks the SE and the interval.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: reading a 95% confidence interval as 'there is a 95% chance the true mean is in this exact interval' or as covering 95% of individuals - it describes the long-run success rate of the method. Mistake: confusing SD (spread of individuals) with SE (spread of sample means). Mistake: ignoring bias - a precise interval from a biased sample is still wrong. Exit: (a) What does the standard error measure, and how does it change with sample size? (b) In one sentence, what does a 95% confidence interval tell you? Answers: the standard error measures how much sample means vary from sample to sample, and it decreases as the sample grows (SE = SD / square root of n); a 95% confidence interval gives a range of plausible values for the parameter, produced by a method that captures the true value about 95% of the time.

lessons.title: Hypothesis testing and common tests
lessons.grammar_note: A small p-value means the data are surprising if the null is true; it does not measure the size or importance of an effect. Report an effect size as well.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Set up null and alternative hypotheses, interpret a p-value, distinguish type I and type II errors, and choose between a t-test and a chi-square test by data type. Warm-up: if a p-value is 0.03 and the threshold is 0.05, do you reject or keep the null?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Hypothesis testing asks whether data are consistent with a default claim. The null hypothesis (H0) says there is no effect or no difference; the alternative (H1) says there is one. You compute a test statistic and a p-value: the probability of data at least as extreme as observed, assuming H0 is true. If the p-value is <= a preset threshold alpha (often 0.05), you reject H0; otherwise you do not reject it. Two errors are possible. A type I error is rejecting a true null - a false positive - and its rate is alpha. A type II error is failing to reject a false null - a false negative - with rate beta; power = 1 - beta is the chance of detecting a real effect, and it rises with sample size. Pick the test by data type. To compare means of a numerical outcome between two groups, use a t-test. To test whether two categorical variables are associated in a table of counts, use a chi-square test. Both convert data into a statistic and a p-value.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: A trial compares the mean blood pressure drop in a drug group versus placebo. H0: the two means are equal; H1: they differ. A two-sample t-test gives p = 0.01. Since 0.01 <= 0.05, reject H0 and conclude the groups differ; still report the actual drop, say 8 mmHg, because significance is not size. A different study asks whether smoking status (yes or no) is associated with having a certain disease (yes or no). That is two categorical variables, so build a 2-by-2 table of counts and run a chi-square test; p = 0.20 > 0.05 means do not reject H0 - no detected association, which is not proof of none. Errors in context: approving a useless drug because the test came out positive by chance is a type I error; missing a drug that truly works because the sample was too small is a type II error. Enrolling more participants raises power and lowers the type II risk.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Write H0 and H1 for 'does drug A change mean weight?' 2) At alpha = 0.05, what do you do with p = 0.08? 3) Which test compares the means of two groups? 4) Which test checks association between two categorical variables? 5) Name the error of rejecting a true null. 6) How do you raise power? Answers: 1) H0: mean weight is unchanged (difference 0); H1: mean weight changes. 2) do not reject H0, since 0.08 > 0.05. 3) a t-test. 4) a chi-square test. 5) a type I error (false positive). 6) increase the sample size (or the true effect size, or alpha).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: reading the p-value as the probability that H0 is true - it is the probability of the data given H0. Mistake: treating 'statistically significant' as 'large' or 'important'; a tiny effect can be significant with a huge sample. Mistake: saying a non-significant result proves no effect, when it may only mean too little power. Exit: (a) Define a type I and a type II error in plain words. (b) Which test fits comparing a numerical outcome between two groups, and which fits two categorical variables? Answers: a type I error is a false positive - rejecting a null that is actually true; a type II error is a false negative - not rejecting a null that is actually false; use a t-test for two group means and a chi-square test for two categorical variables.

items.translation: a measure of spread equal to the typical distance of a value from the mean

items.translation: a range of plausible values for a parameter, from a method that succeeds a set fraction of the time

items.translation: the probability of data at least as extreme as observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true
items.example: A p-value of 0.01 makes the null hypothesis look unlikely.

items.translation: the default claim of no effect or no difference, which a test tries to reject
items.example: H0: the drug and placebo have equal mean effect.

items.translation: the risk of an outcome in an exposed group divided by the risk in an unexposed group
items.example: A relative risk of 2 means the exposed group's risk is doubled.

items.translation: the fraction of truly positive cases that a test correctly flags as positive
items.example: A test with 90% sensitivity misses 10% of the real cases.

lessons.title: Correlation, regression, risk, and reading results responsibly
lessons.grammar_note: Correlation is not causation; a strong r can still come from a confounder. Relative risk suits cohort and trial data, while the odds ratio suits case-control data.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Measure the association between two numerical variables with correlation and a regression line, compute and read risk measures (relative risk, odds ratio, sensitivity, specificity), and judge a result for bias and confounding. Warm-up: ice-cream sales and drowning both rise every summer - what third variable explains both?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Correlation (r) measures the strength and direction of a straight-line relationship between two numerical variables, from -1 (perfect negative) through 0 (none) to +1 (perfect positive). Simple linear regression fits a line, outcome = intercept + slope times predictor, where the slope says how much the outcome changes per one-unit rise in the predictor. Neither proves cause: a lurking confounder can create a strong r. For binary outcomes, risk measures compare groups. Relative risk (RR) is the risk in the exposed divided by the risk in the unexposed; RR = 1 means no difference. The odds ratio (OR) compares odds instead of risks and is the natural measure in case-control studies. For diagnostic tests, sensitivity is the share of true cases correctly flagged positive, and specificity is the share of true non-cases correctly flagged negative; the two trade off against each other. Finally, read every result responsibly: ask whether the sample was biased, whether a confounder could explain the link, whether the effect is large enough to matter, and whether the claim is association or genuine cause.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Correlation and regression: if study hours and exam score have r = 0.8, they rise together strongly, and a regression slope of 4 means each extra hour predicts about 4 more points - prediction, not proof of cause. Relative risk: in a cohort, 20 of 100 exposed get the disease (risk 0.20) versus 10 of 100 unexposed (risk 0.10), so RR = 0.20 / 0.10 = 2.0 - exposure doubles the risk. Odds ratio in a 2-by-2 table with cells a, b, c, d is OR = (a times d) / (b times c); with a = 30, b = 70, c = 10, d = 90, OR = (30 times 90) / (70 times 10) = 2700 / 700, about 3.9. Diagnostic test: of 100 people with the disease, a test flags 90 (sensitivity 90%); of 200 without it, the test clears 180 (specificity 90%). Confounding: ice-cream sales and drowning correlate because hot weather drives both - a classic confounder, not a causal link from dessert to drowning.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) An r of -0.9 describes what kind of relationship? 2) Exposed risk 0.15, unexposed risk 0.05 - find the relative risk. 3) In a test, 80 of 100 true cases are flagged positive - what is the sensitivity? 4) Does a regression slope prove the predictor causes the outcome? 5) Name the confounder behind 'coffee drinkers get more lung cancer.' Answers: 1) a strong negative straight-line relationship. 2) RR = 0.15 / 0.05 = 3.0. 3) 80 / 100 = 80% sensitivity. 4) no - it quantifies association and can be driven by a confounder. 5) smoking, which is more common among coffee drinkers and causes lung cancer.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: reading correlation or a regression slope as proof of cause when a confounder may drive both variables. Mistake: confusing relative risk with the odds ratio, or using RR for a case-control study where only the OR is valid. Mistake: judging a test by sensitivity alone and ignoring specificity, or trusting a precise estimate from a biased sample. Exit: (a) Why does a strong correlation not establish causation? (b) What do sensitivity and specificity each measure? Answers: a third, confounding variable can produce the association without any direct causal link, so correlation only signals that two things move together; sensitivity is the fraction of true positive cases the test correctly flags, and specificity is the fraction of true negatives it correctly clears.
